rows.text:
# How the construction reaches a singular time

Alpöge, Buckmaster and Coiculescu construct smooth periodic initial data for the unforced three-dimensional Euler equations. The velocity stays bounded, while the vorticity at the origin tends to infinity at a finite time. The proof has two connected tasks: amplify a succession of localized waves, and control the corrections needed to make their limit solve Euler. Each finite stage remains an approximate solution.

The route starts with the target, then follows the construction to its limiting solution. The order is explanatory: the parameter schedule appears when it becomes necessary to repeat the construction indefinitely.

rows.label: sec-reading-the-comparisons
rows.text: Each formal statement has been compared with the paper through the full definitions it uses. Theorem 1.1 has the same formal content as the paper, including the torus representation, the norms, maximality and the local limits away from the origin. Where an intermediate result is stronger, the formal version usually weakens a hypothesis, for example by admitting any parent pressure whose residual meets the required bounds. Where it differs, its card names the hypothesis or identification that changes. A stronger verdict for an intermediate estimate does not enlarge Theorem 1.1.

rows.label: sec-step-1-fix-what-must-be-proved
rows.text: Theorem 1.1 concerns a smooth, odd, divergence-free initial velocity on $\mathbb T^3$. Its maximal classical solution has a finite lifespan $[0,T_*)$, bounded velocity and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. Both the gradient and vorticity $L^\infty$ norms have divergent time integrals. Away from the origin, the velocity and its first time derivative have limits in every spatial $C^m$ norm.

rows.label: sec-steps-10-15-build-a-finite-correction-and-preserve-the-hypotheses
rows.text:
At each level, solve for the phase mean first, then for the transverse oscillation, and retain its divergence correction. The order matters because the new mean transports the leading wave's phase. Proposition 5.4 gives an exact identity for the remaining error; Theorem 5.6 bounds that error at a chosen finite depth, with the frequency selected to absorb the constants that depend on the depth.

Lemma 5.8 produces an approximate velocity with two residual terms: the finite expansion remainder and the time cutoff error. Lemma 5.9 controls the added pressure Hessian from above and the error in the central gradient. Lemma 5.10 controls the deformation of the new flow, including after a small perturbation. That separate estimate supplies a hypothesis needed at the next step.

Finally, Proposition 5.11 truncates the velocity in Fourier frequency and estimates the resulting third error. Expansion depth, early wave amplitude and Fourier cutoff control the three errors respectively. The residual remains nonzero at a finite stage. Only the oscillatory part has shrinking support and vanishes before activation; the mean corrections and Fourier tails need not.

rows.label: sec-steps-16-20-use-one-sequence-to-obtain-a-smooth-euler-solution
rows.text:
Lemma 1.3 lets the controlled derivative order $q_j$ tend to infinity slowly enough to absorb the constants required at each stage. Lemma 6.1 starts the construction from a stationary periodic shear. Theorem 7.1 then produces one sequence $U_j$ for all derivative orders, with activation times tending to $T_\infty>0$ and each stage defined beyond that time.

The key estimate (7.4) separates the localized oscillatory increment $O_j$ from $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j$. The velocity increments are summable in the uniform norm. On any fixed interval ending before $T_\infty$, all sufficiently late $O_j$ vanish, and the remaining increments are summable in every fixed spatial derivative norm. Proposition 8.1 passes to the limit in the nonlinear equation as the residual tends to zero. This is where the construction obtains an exact unforced Euler solution.

rows.label: sec-steps-2-6-make-each-wave-prepare-the-next
rows.text:
A Craik–Criminale wave has velocity $\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$, with $\mathbf a\perp k$. Its central gradient is $\mathbf a\otimes k$ when $F'(0)=1$. The preceding wave supplies a shear that amplifies the next wave; the reference equation quantifies this growth. Lemma 2.6 transfers that estimate to the perturbed wave and bounds the evolution of every transverse amplitude, which will also be needed for the corrections.

Large amplitude alone does not make the process repeatable. Proposition 2.8 finds a time when the new wave has the positive couplings and smaller coupling ratio required by its successor, while retaining a large shear. It bounds the wave while it is being switched on by an exponentially small fraction of its attained maximum. The crossing is compared with the reference amplitude maximum; the proposition does not identify the actual amplitude maximum with that time.

Lemma 3.1 chooses a profile with $F_h'(0)=1$ and $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$. When the wave pressure coefficient is positive, these bounds preserve the central gradient while controlling the positive part of the added pressure Hessian. The wave is then localized in particle labels and completed by a curl to preserve incompressibility (§3).

rows.label: sec-steps-21-23-establish-the-terminal-conclusions-separately
rows.text:
Proposition 8.2 proves vorticity growth throughout every sufficiently late activation interval. Projecting along the newest wave vector removes that wave's leading curl and reveals the preceding wave's contribution. This gives a full limit to infinity as $t\uparrow T_\infty$, while the velocity stays bounded.

Corollary 8.3 identifies $T_*=T_\infty$ and proves divergence of both time integrals. Divergence of the vorticity itself would not suffice to prove divergence of its integral. The paper invokes the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda criterion. The formal proof replaces it with an argument specific to the construction: it integrates the quantitative vorticity bound from Proposition 8.2 over the late activation intervals, whose lengths the crossing data bound from below.

For Proposition 8.4, shrinking supports give local spatial limits away from the origin. The first time derivative also requires control of the nonlocal pressure. A spatial cutoff separates the locally controlled term from a distant term whose pressure kernel is smooth. Smooth extension in space and time through the terminal time is the additional conclusion of Remark 1.2.

rows.label: sec-steps-7-9-choose-the-initial-correction-through-an-endpoint-problem
rows.text:
The phase average of the error requires a velocity correction that may extend over the torus. Its initial value is free to change. The construction chooses that initial value so that the first-order change in each particle's final position vanishes.

For the parent flow $X$, write $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. On an interval of length at most one, the upper quadratic-form bound $H^\#\le I$ gives coercivity for displacements vanishing at both endpoints (Lemma 4.1). Large negative eigenvalues are allowed. Theorem 4.2 turns this into an inverse for the linearized endpoint problem, with a bound proportional to the source norm. Lemma 5.3 controls the separate oscillatory equation using the transverse evolution bound. These two inverses solve different parts of the error.

rows.text: ### 2.1 Exact waves over a linear background We first work on $\mathbb R^3$, where linear velocity fields give local models for the periodic construction. Let $D(t)$ be smooth and trace free, with $D'+D^2$ symmetric. Then $Dx$ solves the Euler equations with pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$. Choose a smooth odd $1$-periodic profile $F$ with $F'(0)=1$, and let $P'=F$, $\langle P\rangle_s=0$. Here $\langle H\rangle_s=\int_0^1H(s)\,\mathrm ds$ is the phase average. **Lemma 2.1.** Let the wave vector $k(t)\ne0$ and the amplitude vector $\mathbf a(t)$, functions of time alone, satisfy $$\begin{equation} k'=-D^Tk,\qquad \mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w} k,\qquad p_{\rm w}=\frac{2k\cdot D\mathbf a}{|k|^2},\qquad k\cdot\mathbf a=0. \tag{2.1} \end{equation}$$ Then $Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ is divergence free and solves the Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$ with pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w} P(k\cdot x)$. If $k(t_0)\ne0$, $\mathbf a(t_0)\ne0$ and $k(t_0)\cdot\mathbf a(t_0)=0$, then both vectors remain nonzero and perpendicular for every $t\ge t_0$ in the interval of existence of $D$. *Proof.* Write $w=\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ and $u=Dx+w$. Since $k'=-D^Tk$, $$(\partial_t+Dx\cdot\nabla)(k\cdot x)=(k'+D^Tk)\cdot x=0, \qquad (\partial_t+Dx\cdot\nabla)w=\mathbf a'F.$$ Also $(w\cdot\nabla)Dx=D\mathbf aF$, and perpendicularity cancels the self-advection, $$(w\cdot\nabla)w=(k\cdot\mathbf a)FF'\mathbf a=0.$$ Consequently $$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F.$$ The first term is minus the gradient of the background pressure, and the second equals $p_{\rm w}kF$, which is minus the gradient of the wave pressure $-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$. Moreover $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}D+(k\cdot\mathbf a)F'=0$. The choice of $p_{\rm w}$ gives $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=-2k\cdot D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2=0$. For a given $D$, the equation for $k$ is linear and has an invertible fundamental matrix. Hence $k(t_0)\ne0$ implies $k(t)\ne0$. With this $k$, the equation $\mathbf a'=-(\operatorname{Id}-2\frac{k}{|k|}\frac{k^T}{|k|})D\mathbf a$ is also linear with an invertible fundamental matrix, so $\mathbf a(t_0)\ne0$ implies $\mathbf a(t)\ne0$. $\square$ For a single profile, this is the inviscid wave construction of Craik and Criminale \[[12](#cite-CraikCriminale)\]. #### 2.1.1 The preceding frame A wave evolving over a background matrix $B$ becomes part of the background for the next wave. At the origin, its contribution to the velocity gradient is $\mathbf a\otimes k$, and its unit wave vector and velocity direction provide a moving orthonormal frame. We express the older gradient $B$ in this frame to identify the couplings that drive the next wave. The following calculation uses only $\operatorname{tr}B=0$; it requires no symmetry of $B'+B^2$. **Lemma 2.2.** Let $B(t)$ be a smooth trace-free matrix, and let $k\ne0$ and $\mathbf a\ne0$ satisfy (2.1) with $D$ replaced by $B$. Put $E_1=\frac{k}{|k|}$, $E_2=\frac{\mathbf a}{|\mathbf a|}$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, write $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ $(i,j=1,2,3)$ for the entries of $B$ in this orthonormal frame, and let $\sigma=|k|\,|\mathbf a|$, $\nu=B_{12}$ and $\eta=B_{32}$. Then $$\begin{equation} E_1'=-\nu E_2-B_{13}E_3,\quad E_2'=\nu E_1-\eta E_3,\quad E_3'=B_{13}E_1+\eta E_2, \qquad(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}. \tag{2.2} \end{equation}$$ *Proof.* For an arbitrary nonzero vector $v(t)$ depending on time, put $\widehat v=v/|v|$. In this proof primes denote derivatives in $t$. Then $$\widehat v'=(\operatorname{Id}-\widehat v\widehat v^T)\frac{v'}{|v|},\qquad (\log|v|)'=\widehat v\cdot\frac{v'}{|v|}.$$ Since $B^TE_1=\sum_jB_{1j}E_j$ and $k'=-B^Tk$, this gives $$E_1'=-(\operatorname{Id}-E_1E_1^T)B^TE_1=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3,\qquad (\log|k|)'=-B_{11}.$$ Similarly $BE_2=\sum_iB_{i2}E_i$ and $p_{\rm w}|k|=2|\mathbf a|B_{12}$, so $$E_2'=(\operatorname{Id}-E_2E_2^T)(-BE_2+2B_{12}E_1)=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3, \qquad (\log|\mathbf a|)'=-B_{22}.$$ Using $E_3\times E_2=-E_1$ and $E_1\times E_3=-E_2$ gives $$E_3'=E_1'\times E_2+E_1\times E_2'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2.$$ Finally, $(\log\sigma)'=-B_{11}-B_{22}=B_{33}$ because $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. $\square$ ### 2.2 Amplification on a prescribed interval Of the two entries $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ of the older gradient introduced in Lemma 2.2, the coupling $\nu$ helps the preceding shear amplify a new wave, while $\eta$ changes its direction and eventually ends the growth. A small ratio $\eta/\nu$ therefore allows a large gain before decay. In the model case of Subsection 1.1 and the limit of an infinitely strong preceding shear, the amplitude of a new wave solves a linear system of two equations with explicit coefficients (Lemma 2.3). Up to errors measured by one number $\delta$, the amplitude of a general new wave solves the same system (Lemma 2.4). Its solution with growing initial data peaks after a large gain (Lemma 2.5), and the wave follows this solution with relative errors that grow only polynomially in the length of the interval (Lemma 2.6). The couplings of the new wave are estimated in Lemma 2.7, and Proposition 2.8 locates the ratio prescribed for its successor after the amplitude peaks in the strong-shear limit. #### 2.2.1 The new wave in the preceding frame Let $B(t)$ be a smooth trace-free matrix, and let the preceding wave $(k_p,\mathbf a_p)$, with $k_p\ne0$ and $\mathbf a_p\ne0$, satisfy (2.1) with $D$ replaced by $B$. Let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be its frame, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ the entries of $B$ in this frame, and $\sigma_p=|k_p|\,|\mathbf a_p|$ its strength, as in Lemma 2.2. Thus (2.2) holds with the functions $B_{12}$, $B_{32}$ and $\sigma_p$ in the places of $\nu$, $\eta$ and $\sigma$. The new wave evolves over $$M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c=B+\sigma_p E_2\otimes E_1+E_c,$$ the sum of the older gradient, the gradient of the preceding wave at the origin, and a continuous matrix $E_c(t)$ of errors. Its wave vector $k$ solves the first equation of (2.1) with $D=M$ and equals $\lambda E_3$, with $\lambda>0$, at the activation time $t_0$. For this $k$, an *amplitude vector* is a solution $\mathbf a$ of the second equation in (2.1) with $D=M$ satisfying $\mathbf a(t)\cdot k(t)=0$. Only these ordinary differential equations enter this subsection: the matrices $B$ and $E_c$ are prescribed, and no equation is assumed for them. Subsection 6.2 applies the results below with $M$ the velocity gradient of the parent at the origin, which is a fixed point of the flow. Freeze the strength and the two couplings at the activation time, $$\sigma=\sigma_p(t_0),\qquad \nu=B_{12}(t_0)>0,\qquad \eta=B_{32}(t_0)>0,$$ and put $$r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu},\qquad S=\frac\sigma r=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{2\nu}},\qquad \varepsilon=\frac\eta\nu,\qquad \tau=r(t-t_0).$$ Since $\nu/\sigma=1/(2S^2)$, the growth rate $\sqrt{2\nu(\sigma-\nu)}$ found in Subsection 1.1 equals $r(1-1/(2S^2))^{1/2}$; thus $r$ is this rate up to a factor close to one when $S$ is large. The variable $\tau$ measures time in units of the growth time $r^{-1}$, and $S$ is the ratio of the preceding shear rate to the growth rate. We work on the interval $0\le\tau\le T$, or $t_0\le t\le t_0+T/r$, with $T\ge2$. In (2.1) and (2.2) primes denote derivatives in $t$. From now on in this subsection they denote derivatives in $\tau$, so that $d/d\tau=r^{-1}d/dt$. All suprema are over $0\le\tau\le T$, and $b_{ij}=B_{ij}/r$. Define the scaled components $\zeta=(\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\zeta_3)$ and $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ of the wave vector and an amplitude vector by $$\begin{equation} k=\lambda\left(\zeta_1E_1+\frac{\zeta_2}{S}E_2+\zeta_3E_3\right), \qquad \mathbf a=\frac{\alpha_1}{S}E_1+\alpha_2E_2+\frac{\alpha_3}{S}E_3. \tag{2.3} \end{equation}$$ Then $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ and $$|k|^2=\lambda^2m,\qquad m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2.$$ Transversality is $\zeta\cdot\alpha=0$, so where $\zeta_3\ne0$, $$\alpha_3=-\frac{\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2}{\zeta_3}.$$ The two components $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ therefore determine the amplitude vector. The factor $S^{-1}$ in the $E_2$ coordinate of $k$ makes the contribution of $B$ to the coefficient of $\zeta_3$ in the equation for $\zeta_2$ equal to $-B_{32}/\nu$, which equals $-\varepsilon$ at $\tau=0$. In the growing mode of Subsection 1.1, the components of the amplitude along $E_1$ and $E_2$ have opposite signs, and the first is $S^{-1}(1-\nu/\sigma)^{-1/2}$ times the second in absolute value. With the scaling in (2.3), this mode is $\alpha_1=-\alpha_2$ to leading order. In Subsection 2.2.2 the components $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ are divided further by the amplitude in the strong-shear limit, which gives the normalized coordinates (2.15). In the model case of Subsection 1.1, the entries of $B$ in the frame are the constants $B_{12}=\nu$ and $B_{32}=\eta$, all other entries vanish, and $E_c=0$. Put $$\begin{equation} \tan\varphi=\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau^2,\qquad 0\le\varphi<\tfrac\pi2,\qquad \zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1). \tag{2.4} \end{equation}$$ The next lemma derives the equations for the scaled components in the model case and their limit as the preceding shear becomes infinitely strong. In the limit the wave vector is $\lambda(\tan\varphi E_1+E_3)$, so $\varphi$ is its angle from $E_3$ toward $E_1$, as in Subsection 1.1. **Lemma 2.3.** Suppose that on $0\le\tau\le T$ the entries of $B$ in the frame are $B_{12}=\nu$, $B_{32}=\eta$ and $B_{ij}=0$ otherwise, and that $E_c=0$. Then $\sigma_p=\sigma$, and the scaled components of the wave vector satisfy $$\zeta_1'=-\Bigl(1+\frac1{2S^2}\Bigr)\zeta_2,\qquad \zeta_2'=-\varepsilon\zeta_3,\qquad \zeta_3'=\frac{\varepsilon}{2S^2}\zeta_2 .$$ Where $\zeta_3\ne0$, the components $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ of every amplitude vector satisfy $$\begin{aligned} \alpha_1'&=-\alpha_2+\zeta_1\Pi,\\ \alpha_2'&=-\Bigl(1-\frac1{2S^2}\Bigr)\alpha_1 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2S^2}\,\frac{\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2}{\zeta_3} +\frac{\zeta_2}{S^2}\,\Pi, \end{aligned} \qquad \Pi=\frac{2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2}m .$$ As $S\to\infty$ with $\varepsilon$ and $T$ fixed, $\zeta\to\zeta_0$ uniformly on $[0,T]$, and the coefficients of this system for $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ converge uniformly on $[0,T]$ to those of $$\begin{equation} \alpha_1'=-\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\alpha_2 -\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,\alpha_1, \qquad \alpha_2'=-\alpha_1 . \tag{2.5} \end{equation}$$ *Proof.* In this proof write $k_i=k\cdot E_i$ and $a_i=\mathbf a\cdot E_i$, and let a dot denote the derivative in $t$. The frame equations (2.2) read $\dot E_1=-\nu E_2$, $\dot E_2=\nu E_1-\eta E_3$ and $\dot E_3=\eta E_2$, and their last equation gives $d(\log\sigma_p)/dt=B_{33}=0$, so $\sigma_p=\sigma$. Thus $M=\nu E_1\otimes E_2+\eta E_3\otimes E_2+\sigma E_2\otimes E_1$, and $ME_1=\sigma E_2$, $ME_2=\nu E_1+\eta E_3$, $ME_3=0$. Since $\dot k=-M^Tk$, we have $\dot k_i=-k\cdot ME_i+k\cdot\dot E_i$, hence $$\dot k_1=-(\sigma+\nu)k_2,\qquad \dot k_2=-2\eta k_3,\qquad \dot k_3=\eta k_2 .$$ Since $\dot{\mathbf a}=-M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$ and $M\mathbf a=\nu a_2E_1+\sigma a_1E_2+\eta a_2E_3$, also $\dot a_i=-E_i\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k_i+\mathbf a\cdot\dot E_i$, hence $$\dot a_1=-2\nu a_2+p_{\rm w}k_1,\qquad \dot a_2=-(\sigma-\nu)a_1-\eta a_3+p_{\rm w}k_2,\qquad p_{\rm w}=\frac{2(\nu k_1a_2+\sigma k_2a_1+\eta k_3a_2)}{|k|^2}.$$ Substitute (2.3), divide by $r$ to pass to the time $\tau$, and use $$rS=\sigma,\qquad \frac{\nu}{\sigma}=\frac1{2S^2},\qquad \frac{\nu S}r=\frac12,\qquad \frac{\eta S}r=\frac\varepsilon2,\qquad \frac\eta\sigma=\frac{\varepsilon}{2S^2}.$$ The equations for $k_i$ give those for $\zeta$, and $\lambda Sp_{\rm w}/r=\Pi$. The equations for $a_1$ and $a_2$ then give those for $\alpha_1=Sa_1$ and $\alpha_2=a_2$, after substituting $\alpha_3=-(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/\zeta_3$. As $S\to\infty$, the coefficients of the system for $\zeta$ converge to those of $\zeta_1'=-\zeta_2$, $\zeta_2'=-\varepsilon\zeta_3$, $\zeta_3'=0$, whose solution with $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ is $\zeta_0$. Both systems are linear with bounded coefficients on $[0,T]$, so $\zeta\to\zeta_0$ uniformly there by Gronwall’s inequality. In particular $\zeta_3\to1$ and $m\to1+\tan^2\varphi=\cos^{-2}\varphi$. In the equation for $\alpha_1$ the coefficients of $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ therefore converge to $$\frac{2\zeta_1\zeta_2}m\to-2\varepsilon\tau\tan\varphi\cos^2\varphi =-\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi,\qquad -1+\frac{\zeta_1(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)}m \to-\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi),$$ since $(\tan\varphi+\varepsilon)\tan\varphi\cos^2\varphi =\sin^2\varphi+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$. In the equation for $\alpha_2$ every term except $-\alpha_1$ has a factor $S^{-2}$ and a bounded coefficient, so the two coefficients converge to $-1$ and $0$. $\square$ We call (2.5) the *reference system*. The vector $\zeta_0$ solves the limiting system $\zeta_1'=-\zeta_2$, $\zeta_2'=-\varepsilon\zeta_3$, $\zeta_3'=0$ for the wave vector. The errors of the comparison are measured by $$\begin{equation} \delta=\left\|\frac{B_{12}}{\nu}-1\right\|_\infty +\left\|\frac{B_{32}}{\eta}-1\right\|_\infty +\frac{\|B\|_\infty}{r}+\frac{\|E_c\|_\infty}{\nu}. \tag{2.6} \end{equation}$$ The first two terms are the relative variations of the two couplings on the interval. The third compares the older gradient with the growth rate; it is at least $\nu/r=1/(2S)$, as shown below, so it is small only if the preceding shear is strong. The last compares the error $E_c$ with the coupling $\nu$ rather than with $r$. The scaled components multiply the $E_2$ component of $k$ and the $E_1$ and $E_3$ components of $\mathbf a$ by $S$, so in the time $\tau$ an entry of $E_c$ enters their equations with a factor up to $S/r=1/(2\nu)$; see the proof of Lemma 2.4. Fix an absolute constant $C_0$, sufficiently large for the finitely many estimates of this subsection, and assume $$\begin{equation} C_0\varepsilon\le1,\qquad C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon . \tag{2.7} \end{equation}$$ All other constants and exponents $C,c$ in this subsection are absolute and do not depend on $C_0$; they may change from one estimate to the next. The errors below have the form $CT^C\delta$, and by (2.7) such an error is at most $\varepsilon$ times any prescribed negative power of $T$ once $C_0$ is large. Condition (2.7) forces the preceding shear to be strong. Indeed, $|B|\ge|E_1\cdot BE_2|$, and at $\tau=0$ this entry is $B_{12}(t_0)=\nu$. Since $\nu/r=\sqrt{\nu/(2\sigma)}=1/(2S)$, the third term of (2.6) gives $\delta\ge\nu/r=1/(2S)$. On the other hand, (2.7) gives $\delta\le\varepsilon C_0^{-1}T^{-C_0}\le C_0^{-2}T^{-C_0}$. For $C_0\ge2$ and $T\ge2$ it follows that $$\begin{equation} S\ge\frac1{2\delta}\ge\frac{C_0^2T^{C_0}}2\ge T^2,\qquad S^{-2}\le4\delta^2\le\delta, \tag{2.8} \end{equation}$$ where the last inequality uses $\delta\le1/4$. In the applications in Subsection 6.2 and Section 7, the parameter choice (1.14) prescribes $\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $T$ are bounded by powers of the logarithm of the frequency of the preceding wave, while $\delta$ is at most a negative power of that frequency times a power of its logarithm. Item 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1 verifies (2.7) in this way. Its growing solutions have $\alpha_1=-\alpha_2$, the direction $-E_1/S+E_2$ of the amplitude in (2.3). As $\varphi$ increases, the pressure reduces the coefficient driving $\alpha_1$ from one to $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)$ and introduces the term $-\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,\alpha_1$. The driving coefficient becomes negative when $\varepsilon\tan\varphi>1$. The *reference solution* is the solution of the reference system with $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)(0)=(-1,1)$, shown in Figure 1. A later wave is started with these data in Subsection 6.2. The second equation of (2.5), $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$, holds at every $\tau$. Hence, wherever $\alpha_2>0$, the logarithmic derivative of $\alpha_2$ is $$Y=\frac{\alpha_2'}{\alpha_2}=-\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2},$$ and the first equation of (2.5) gives the Riccati equation $$\begin{equation} Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi) -\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,Y-Y^2,\qquad Y(0)=1. \tag{2.12} \end{equation}$$ Conversely, if $Y$ solves (2.12), then $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ is the reference solution, where $$a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\left(\int_0^\tau Y(\tau')\,d\tau'\right).$$ We call $a_{\rm ref}$ the *reference amplitude*. **Lemma 2.5.** Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The solution $Y$ of (2.12) exists for all $\tau\ge0$, satisfies $|Y|\le1$, and has the form $$\begin{equation} Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\tfrac14\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi, \qquad 0\le e\le\tfrac18\varepsilon. \tag{2.13} \end{equation}$$ The reference amplitude satisfies $$\begin{equation} a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(\tau)} \exp\left(\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi\,d\tau'\right). \tag{2.14} \end{equation}$$ The function $Y$ has exactly one zero $\tau_m$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$. It is positive before this zero and negative afterwards, so $a_{\rm ref}$ is largest at $\tau_m$, and $$\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1.$$ *Proof.* Since $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $$\varphi'=\varepsilon\tau\cos^2\varphi,\qquad (\log\cos\varphi)'=-\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi.$$ We look for $Y$ in the form (2.13), an ansatz with an unknown function $e$. To motivate it, write $Y=\cos\varphi+w$, where $\cos\varphi$ is the positive equilibrium of the equation $Y'=\cos^2\varphi-Y^2$ with $\varphi$ frozen. Neglecting $w'$, $w^2$, $\varepsilon\tau w\sin2\varphi$ and the term $-\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$ of order $\varepsilon$, (2.12) reduces to $2w\cos\varphi=-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi\cos^2\varphi$, that is, $w=-\tfrac14\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi=\tfrac12(\log\cos\varphi)'$. The factor $1+e$ absorbs the neglected terms. Integrating (2.13) and using the formula for $(\log\cos\varphi)'$ gives (2.14). Substituting (2.13) into (2.12) gives $$e'=\cos\varphi\bigl(-2e-e^2 +\tfrac12\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\bigr), \qquad e(0)=0.$$ The right-hand side is nonnegative at $e=0$ and nonpositive at $e=\varepsilon/8$, because $\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\le1/2$. Hence $e$ remains in $[0,\varepsilon/8]$ and exists for all $\tau\ge0$. This constructs the global solution $Y$. Wherever $Y\ge0$, (2.12) gives $Y'\le1-Y^2$, because $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\le1$. Since $Y(0)=1$, $Y(\tau)$ never exceeds one. Also $\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\le\min\{1/2,\cot\varphi\}$, so for $\tau>0$, $$\tfrac14\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi \le\min\{\varepsilon\tau/4,1/\tau\}\le\tfrac12.$$ Equation (2.13) therefore gives $Y\ge-1/2$. Write $Y=\cos\varphi(1+e-\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi)$. It is positive for $\varepsilon\tau\le2$, because $e\ge0$ and $\sin\varphi<1$. For $\varepsilon\tau=3$, we have $\tan\varphi=9/(2\varepsilon)\ge9/2$, hence $\sin\varphi>3/4$ and $\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi>9/8\ge1+e$. Thus $Y$ is negative there. At any zero with $\varepsilon\tau\ge2$, $$Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi) =\cos^2\varphi\bigl(1-(\varepsilon\tau)^2/2\bigr)<0.$$ Consequently $Y$ has exactly one zero $\tau_m$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$, and has the stated signs on its two sides. For $0\le\tau\le(2/\varepsilon)^{1/2}$, we have $\tan\varphi\le1$, hence $\cos\varphi\ge2^{-1/2}$. This interval ends before $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$, where $a_{\rm ref}$ is largest. By (2.14) and $e\ge0$, $$\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m) \ge\log a_{\rm ref}\bigl((2/\varepsilon)^{1/2}\bigr) \ge2^{-1/2}(2/\varepsilon)^{1/2}-\tfrac14\log2 \ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1.$$ $\square$ Relative to the reference solution, the reference system is triangular. To compare a solution $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ of (2.5) with the reference solution $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$, we divide by the reference amplitude, which removes the exponential growth common to the growing solutions, and we separate the size of $\alpha_2$ from the deviation of the ratio $\alpha_1/\alpha_2$ from its reference value $-Y$. We call $$\begin{equation} h=\frac{\alpha_2}{a_{\rm ref}},\qquad l=-\frac{\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2}{a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi} \tag{2.15} \end{equation}$$ the *normalized coordinates* of $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. The factor $1/\cos\varphi$ in $l$ gives the equations for $h$ and $l$ below the same factor $\cos\varphi$, which yields a propagator bound uniform in $\varepsilon$ and in the length of the interval. By the second equation of (2.5) and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$, we have $h'=l\cos\varphi$. The trace of the reference coefficient matrix is $-\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi=2(\log\cos\varphi)'$. By Liouville’s formula, the determinant $$\det\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_1&-Ya_{\rm ref}\\ \alpha_2&a_{\rm ref}\end{pmatrix} =a_{\rm ref}(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)=-a_{\rm ref}^2l\cos\varphi$$ is a constant multiple of $\cos^2\varphi$. Formula (2.14) thus gives $$l(\tau)=l(0)\exp\left(-2\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi\,d\tau'\right).$$ The reference system becomes $$\begin{equation} h'=l\cos\varphi,\qquad l'=-2(1+e)l\cos\varphi, \tag{2.16} \end{equation}$$ and the reference solution is $(h,l)=(1,0)$. The second equation shows that $|l|$ does not increase. A direct Gronwall estimate for $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ would introduce $\exp(CT)$, while (2.7) controls polynomial losses in $T$. Their large parts cancel. To see this, write $Y=(1+e-u)\cos\varphi$ by (2.13), with $u=\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi$, so that $2\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi=4u$ and $2u^2=\varepsilon\tan\varphi\sin^2\varphi$. Dividing the second expression by $\cos\varphi$ gives $$\begin{align*} &(\varepsilon\tan\varphi-1)+2(1+e-u)^2+4u(1+e-u)\\ &\qquad=\varepsilon\tan\varphi-1 +\bigl[2(1+e)^2-4u(1+e)+2u^2\bigr]+\bigl[4u(1+e)-4u^2\bigr]\\ &\qquad=1+4e+2e^2+\bigl(\varepsilon\tan\varphi-2u^2\bigr). \end{align*}$$ The terms $\pm4u(1+e)$ cancel, and the large parts of $\varepsilon\tan\varphi$ and $2u^2$ cancel: $$\varepsilon\tan\varphi-2u^2=\varepsilon\tan\varphi\,(1-\sin^2\varphi) =\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\le\tfrac12\varepsilon .$$ Similarly, $2\varepsilon\tau Y\cos\varphi =2(1+e)\varepsilon\tau\cos^2\varphi -2\varepsilon\sin^2\varphi\cos\varphi$. Thus the reference values of $\nu_+/\nu$ and $\eta_+/\nu$ are $$\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi\cos2\varphi +2(1+e)\varepsilon\tau\cos^2\varphi,\\ (1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi)\cos\varphi. \end{gathered} \tag{2.22} \end{equation}$$ Where $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\ge1$, we have $\cos\varphi\le\cot\varphi\le\varepsilon$, so $1-\varepsilon^2\le\sin\varphi\le1$. Also $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ and $$\varepsilon\tau\cos^2\varphi \le\varepsilon\tau\cot^2\varphi =\frac4{\varepsilon\tau^3}\le\sqrt2\,\varepsilon^2.$$ The two reference values in (2.22) are $1+O(\varepsilon^2)$ and $(1+O(\varepsilon))\cos\varphi$. Where $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\le1$, we have $\varepsilon\tau\le\sqrt2$, hence $Y>0$ by Lemma 2.5. The unsimplified reference value of $\nu_+/\nu$ is at least $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi \ge\varepsilon$. For the wave, in (2.20)–(2.21), the coefficients differ from their reference values by at most $CT\delta$; $\zeta$ differs from $\zeta_0$ by at most $CT^C\delta$; the terms with $S^{-2}$ in those formulas, in $m$ and in $n$, are at most $CT^C\delta$; and $q$ differs from $-Y$ by at most $CT^C\delta$, by (2.17). The formula for $z$ and the bound $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ give the same bound for its change. The numerators are polynomials of bounded degree in these quantities and $1/\zeta_3$, which are at most $CT^2$, while the denominators $\sqrt m\,n$ and $\sqrt m\,n^2$ are at least $1/2$. Together with the contribution of $E_c$, the two ratios therefore differ from their reference values by at most $CT^C\delta$, which is at most $\varepsilon T^{-2}/8$ by (2.7). In both ranges the reference value of $\nu_+/\nu$ is at least $\varepsilon$; in the late range this uses $C_0\varepsilon\le1$. Hence $\nu_+/\nu\ge\varepsilon/2$ on the whole interval. In the late range, $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$. Combining the perturbation bounds with (2.22) gives $$\left|\frac{\nu_+}{\nu}-1\right|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \frac{\eta_+}{\nu_+}=(1+O(\varepsilon))\cos\varphi.$$ The latter gives (2.19) for $C_0$ sufficiently large. $\square$ #### 2.2.5 The crossing After the peak of the reference solution at $\tau_m$, the new wave becomes the shear for the next wave, whose coupling ratio $\varepsilon_+$ is prescribed in advance. By (2.19), the coupling ratio $\eta_+/\nu_+$ of the new wave is comparable to $\cos\varphi$. It therefore reaches $\varepsilon_+$ when $\cos\varphi$ is comparable to $\varepsilon_+$, that is, when $\tan\varphi$ is comparable to $1/\varepsilon_+$, or $\tau$ to $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. We call a time $\tau$ at which $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$ a *crossing*: there the ratio reaches the threshold $\varepsilon_+$ prescribed for the next wave. The next wave is activated at a crossing. The reference amplitude decreases after $\tau_m$, and the wave-vector length is comparable to $\lambda/\cos\varphi$. The next proposition bounds their product for the actual wave at a crossing, and shows that its amplitude is small compared with its maximum during the first unit of normalized time. The strength $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a||k|$ at the crossing and the coupling $\nu_+$ supply the frozen parameters $\sigma,\nu$ for the next wave. **Proposition 2.8.** Assume (2.7), let $\mathbf a$ be the amplitude vector of Lemma 2.6, with the couplings of Lemma 2.7, and suppose that $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $T\ge2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. Then the interval $\tau_m\le\tau\le2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$, where $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$ is the zero of $Y$ (Lemma 2.5), contains a crossing. At every crossing in this interval the strength $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a(\tau)||k(\tau)|$ satisfies $$\begin{equation} C^{-1}(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2} \le\frac{\sigma_+}{\lambda\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|} \le C(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}. \tag{2.23} \end{equation}$$ Moreover $$\begin{equation} |\mathbf a(\tau)|\le\exp\bigl(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}\bigr) \max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|\qquad(0\le\tau\le1). \tag{2.24} \end{equation}$$ *Proof.* By Lemma 2.5, $2/\varepsilon\le\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$, we have $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}\ge4/\varepsilon$. Thus $\tau_m<2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}\le T$, and $[\tau_m,T]$ lies in the range $\tau\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$ of (2.19). For $\tau_m\le\tau\le T$, we have $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2\ge2/\varepsilon\ge1$, hence $$\frac1{2\tan\varphi}\le\cos\varphi\le\frac1{\tan\varphi},\qquad \frac1{4\tan\varphi}\le\frac{\eta_+}{\nu_+}\le\frac3{2\tan\varphi},$$ by (2.19). At $\tau_m$, $\tan\varphi\le9/(2\varepsilon)$, so $\eta_+/\nu_+\ge\varepsilon/18>\varepsilon_+$. At $\tau=2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$, we have $\tan\varphi=2/\varepsilon_+$, so $\eta_+/\nu_+\le3\varepsilon_+/4<\varepsilon_+$. Continuity therefore gives a crossing in this interval. At every crossing in $[\tau_m,T]$ the displayed bounds give $1/(4\varepsilon_+)\le\tan\varphi\le3/(2\varepsilon_+)$, so $\cos\varphi$ is comparable to $\varepsilon_+$. To estimate the strength at a crossing, we compare the amplitude there with its maximum on $[0,T]$. By (2.18), $|\mathbf a|$ lies between $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$ and $\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$. The maximum of $a_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$ is attained at $\tau_m$, so for $\tau_m\le\tau\le T$, $|\mathbf a(\tau)|/\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ is bounded above and below by absolute multiples of $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$. Formula (2.14) gives $$\frac{a_{\rm ref}(\tau)}{a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)} =\left(\frac{\cos\varphi(\tau)}{\cos\varphi(\tau_m)}\right)^{1/2} \exp\left(\int_{\tau_m}^{\tau}(1+e)\cos\varphi\,d\tau'\right).$$ The integral lies between zero and two, since $\int_{\tau_m}^\infty\cos\varphi\,d\tau\le2/(\varepsilon\tau_m)\le1$. Also $|k|$ is comparable to $\lambda/\cos\varphi$, by (2.10). Thus $\sigma_+/(\lambda\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|)$ is comparable to $(\cos\varphi(\tau)\cos\varphi(\tau_m))^{-1/2}$. Here $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)$ is comparable to $\varepsilon$, because $2/\varepsilon\le\tan\varphi(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$, and at a crossing $\cos\varphi$ is comparable to $\varepsilon_+$. This proves (2.23). For $0\le\tau\le1$, the bound $Y\le1$ gives $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)\le\exp(\tau)\le\exp(1)$, while $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$ by Lemma 2.5. By (2.18) at such $\tau$ and at $\tau_m$, $|\mathbf a(\tau)|\le\exp(1+\varepsilon)$ and $|\mathbf a(\tau_m)|\ge\exp(\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1-\varepsilon)$. Since $2\varepsilon\le1$, this gives (2.24). $\square$

rows.text: On the common interval $[0,T_\infty]$ of Theorem 7.1, (7.4) gives $\|U_j-U_{j-1}\|_{C_tL^\infty} \le2\lambda_j^{-1}$. The sum converges, so the velocities converge uniformly to a continuous field $w$ on $[0,T_\infty]\times\mathbb T^3$. For convergence of derivatives we use that the oscillations vanish before activation and have supports shrinking to the origin. ### 8.1 Convergence before the accumulation time **Proposition 8.1.** The data $U_j(0)$ converge in every $C^{m,1/2}$ to an odd divergence-free field $u_0$. In particular, $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$. Let $u$ be the maximal smooth solution of the Euler equations from $u_0$, with maximal time $T_*>0$, supplied by Section 1. Then $T_*\ge T_\infty$ and, for every $Tj_0$ the oscillation $O_j$ vanishes on $[0,T]$. Thus (7.4) gives, for $\ell>n\ge j_0$, $$\|U_\ell-U_n\|_{C([0,T];C^{m,1/2})} \le\sum_{j>n}\lambda_j^{-1}\le2\lambda_{n+1}^{-1}.$$ The limit in each of these norms is $w$. In particular $u_0=w(0)$ is smooth, and $w$ is odd and divergence free on $[0,T]$. Integrating (7.5) gives $$U_j(t)=U_j(0)-\int_0^t\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(U_j\otimes U_j)\,\mathrm dt' +\int_0^tR_j\,\mathrm dt'.$$ By (T2), the last integral has supremum norm at most $T\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$. Convergence in $C([0,T];C^{1,1/2})$, the product estimate (5.59) and boundedness of $\mathbb P$ on $C^{0,1/2}$ give uniform convergence of the projected nonlinear term. Hence $\partial_t w=-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(w\otimes w)$. The right-hand side is continuous in every spatial Hölder norm, so differentiating the equation gives joint smoothness. Uniqueness identifies $w$ with $u$ wherever both exist. Since $w$ exists for every $T ### 8.2 Velocity, central vorticity and the maximal time **Proposition 8.2.** The solution has bounded velocity on $[0,T_\infty)$, and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\longrightarrow\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_\infty$. *Proof.* The continuous field $w$ on $[0,T_\infty]\times\mathbb T^3$ is bounded, and Proposition 8.1 identifies it with $u$ before $T_\infty$. For the vorticity, fix a large $j$ and consider the whole interval $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$. The preceding wave is fully active there. Applying (T4) of Theorem 7.1 at steps $j-1$ and $j$ gives, at the origin, $$\nabla U_j=\nabla U_{j-2} +\mathbf a_{j-1}\otimes\kappa_{j-1} +\widetilde\chi_j\,\mathbf a_j\otimes\kappa_j+E_{c,j-1}+E_{c,j}.$$ A gradient $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ contributes $\kappa\times\mathbf a$ to vorticity. Projecting $\operatorname{curl}U_j$ along $\kappa_j$ therefore removes the leading curl of wave $j$. The preceding wave contributes $\kappa_{j-1}\times\mathbf a_{j-1}=\sigma_{j-1}E_3$ in its own frame. By (2.3) and Lemma 2.4, the $E_3$ component of $\kappa_j/\lambda_j$ is at least $1/2$ and its length is at most $C(1+\tau^2)$ at normalized time $\tau$. The normalized length of $[t_j,S_j]$ is at most $CL_{j+1}^4$ by item 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1. Thus $$\begin{equation} \frac{\kappa_j}{|\kappa_j|}\cdot(\kappa_{j-1}\times\mathbf a_{j-1}) \ge c\sigma_{j-1}L_{j+1}^{-8},\qquad \frac{\kappa_j}{|\kappa_j|}\cdot(\kappa_j\times\mathbf a_j)=0. \tag{8.1} \end{equation}$$ The preceding wave retains its strength throughout $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$. Put $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. At $t_j$, (7.3) gives $\sigma_{j-1}\ge c\mu^{1/4}$. By (2.2), $|\partial_t\log\sigma_{j-1}|\le|\nabla U_{j-2}(t,0)| \le\lambda_{j-2}^9\le\mu^{1/32}$, using (7.6) and item 2 above. Since the interval has length at most $\tau_j\le\mu^{-1/16}$ by (T4) and (7.7), $\log\sigma_{j-1}$ changes by at most one. Hence $\sigma_{j-1}\ge c\mu^{1/4}$ on the whole interval. Since $L_{j+1}^8\le(\log\mu)^{16}\le\mu^{1/8}$ for large $j$ by (1.15), the projected curl of the preceding wave in (8.1) is at least $c\mu^{1/8}$. The older gradient contributes at most $C\lambda_{j-2}^9$ to the curl and the two central errors are at most $2\mu^{-1/4}$ in norm. Consequently $$\begin{equation} |\operatorname{curl}U_j(t,0)| \ge c\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}-C\lambda_{j-2}^9-C, \tag{8.2} \end{equation}$$ which tends to infinity uniformly on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$. For $\ell>j$ the oscillation $O_\ell$ vanishes throughout $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$. Applying (7.4) to the remaining increments at order one and taking the limit by Proposition 8.1 gives $$\sup_{t_j\le t\le t_{j+1}}|\operatorname{curl}(u-U_j)(t,0)| \le C\sum_{\ell>j}\lambda_\ell^{-1}.$$ This tail tends to zero. The successive intervals cover $[t_j,T_\infty)$, so (8.2) gives $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_\infty$. $\square$ **Corollary 8.3.** The maximal existence time is $T_*=T_\infty\in(0,\infty)$, and both integrals in (1.2) diverge. *Proof.* By Proposition 8.1, $T_*\ge T_\infty$. If $T_*>T_\infty$, then smoothness on the compact interval $[0,T_\infty]$ would bound $\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)$, contrary to Proposition 8.2. Hence $T_*=T_\infty$, which is positive and finite by Theorem 7.1. The initial data are smooth, so the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda criterion \[[9](#cite-BKM)\], in the formulation of \[[11](#cite-GGPP), Theorem 1\], implies $\int_0^{T_*}\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty\,\mathrm dt=\infty$. The gradient integral also diverges, since $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty\le C\|\nabla u\|_\infty$. $\square$ ### 8.3 The velocity away from the origin at the singular time **Proposition 8.4.** For every compact $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ and every integer $m\ge0$, both $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ converge in $C^m(K)$ as $t\uparrow T_\infty$. *Proof.* Fix $K$ and $m$ as in the statement. The support of $O_j$ lies in the ball of radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ about the origin throughout $[0,T_\infty]$. For large $j$ the ball is disjoint from $K$ and $q_j\ge m$, so (7.4) gives $\|U_j-U_{j-1}\|_{C([0,T_\infty];C^m(K))}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$. The increments are summable in this norm, hence $u(t)\to w(T_\infty)$ in $C^m(K)$. The time derivative also contains the pressure gradient, which depends on the velocity on the whole torus. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $K$ and zero near the origin. On $[0,T_\infty)$ we have $$\partial_tu=-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(\chi u\otimes u)-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl((1-\chi)u\otimes u\bigr).$$ Applying the spatial convergence just proved on $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ through order $m+2$ gives convergence of $\chi u\otimes u$ in $C^{m+1,1/2}$ on the torus. Since $\mathbb P\operatorname{div}$ maps $C^{m+1,1/2}$ boundedly to $C^{m,1/2}$, the first term converges in $C^m(K)$. For the second term, $\operatorname{supp}(1-\chi)$ is a positive distance from $K$. Only the pressure part $-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div}$ acts across this distance. Its kernel is smooth off the diagonal, so for any bounded tensor field $A$, $$\|\mathbb P\operatorname{div}((1-\chi)A)\|_{C^m(K)}\le C_{m,K,\chi}\|A\|_{L^1}.$$ Since $u(t)\otimes u(t)\to w(T_\infty)\otimes w(T_\infty)$ uniformly on the torus, the difference tends to zero in $L^1$. The estimate therefore gives convergence of the second term in $C^m(K)$. $\square$ Propositions 8.1, 8.2 and 8.4 and Corollary 8.3 prove Theorem 1.1.

The construction of Craik–Criminale waves on the torus can be chosen so that the velocity extends smoothly in space and time through the singular time away from the origin. We give the additional estimates for this strengthening of the terminal conclusion in the main paper.
### Note 1 Choice of $\mathcal B$ and the stronger conclusion We use the notation and the construction of *Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations*. References with prefix M refer to that paper. **Theorem 1.1.** The function $\mathcal B$ of Subsection M.1.5 may be chosen so that the restriction of the solution in Theorem M.1.1 to $[0,T_*)\times(\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\})$ extends to a smooth field on an open space-time neighborhood of $\{T_*\}\times(\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\})$. All other conclusions of that theorem remain unchanged. The Euler equations are imposed only for $0\le t(M.1.13) and such that, for every integer $s\ge1$, $\mathcal B(s)$ bounds the fixed-order constants of the paper at orders and depths at most $7K(s)$. We choose one for which $\mathcal B(s)$ also bounds the constants in the time-derivative estimates below with all derivative orders and the depth at most $7K(s)$. These quantities depend only on the orders and the depth: the estimates below display dependence on the previous frequency parameter as fixed powers and contain no constant depending on the constructed solution. The function $\mathcal B$ is chosen before the initial frequency parameter $N$, and the orders $q_j$ and the frequencies are defined by (M.1.14) with it. Lemma M.1.3 applies to this choice, and the construction and the main theorem are obtained with it. Thus the orders satisfy $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$ and $q_j\to\infty$, and $$\begin{equation} \mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\lambda_{j-1}. \tag{1.1} \end{equation}$$ The additional estimates concern the fields $U_j$ of this construction. As in Section M.7, $O_j$ is the oscillation of step $j$ and $R_j$ is the residual of $U_j$. The fields of step $j$ are defined on $[0,S_j]$, and $S_j>T_\infty=T_*$. **Lemma 1.2.** For all integers $m,q\ge0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, $$\begin{equation} \|\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)\|_{C([0,S_j];C^{m,1/2})} \le\lambda_j^{-1}. \tag{1.2} \end{equation}$$ The time derivatives are taken at fixed spatial point. The starting index may depend on $(m,q)$. By (M.7.5) the time derivatives of $U_j$ involve those of $R_j$; the next lemma bounds both. The residual of $U_j$ is built in step $j$ from the parent $U_{j-1}$, and at time order $q$ it uses the residual of that parent only to time order $q-1$. This is why the induction on the time order closes. **Lemma 1.3.** For every integer $q\ge0$ there are an exponent $\psi_q$ and an index $j_q$, depending only on $q$ and the fixed construction, such that for $j\ge j_q$ and $0\le i\le q$, $$\begin{equation} \|\partial_t^iU_j\|_{C([0,S_j];L^\infty)}\le\lambda_j^{\psi_q},\qquad \|\partial_t^iR_j\|_{C([0,S_j];L^\infty)}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}. \tag{1.3} \end{equation}$$ The fields $\partial_t^iU_j$ and $\partial_t^iR_j$ are supported on frequencies at most $2\Lambda_j$ and $4\Lambda_j$. Thus (M.B.1) and (1.3) bound every spatial derivative of these fields: a derivative of order $m$ costs $C_m\Lambda_j^m=C_m\lambda_j^{5m}$. ### Note 2 Time derivatives of the increments *Proof of Lemmas 1.2 and 1.3.* We argue by induction on $q$. For $q=0$, Lemma 1.2 is the second bound of (M.7.4), which holds as soon as $q_j\ge m$, and (1.3) is (T2) of Theorem M.7.1, with $\psi_0=1$ and $j_0=1$. Let $q\ge1$, and assume Lemma 1.3 with $q-1$ in place of $q$. We prove Lemma 1.2 for this $q$ and every $m$, and then Lemma 1.3 for $q$. Let $j-1\ge j_{q-1}$, and write $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ and $\lambda=\lambda_j$. Put $T=S_j$, $U=U_{j-1}$, $R_U=R_{j-1}$, $\Lambda_U=\Lambda_{j-1}=\mu^5$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. Below, all exponents depend only on $q$, on $m$ once it enters, and on the fixed construction; constants $C_q$ may depend also on the label and phase order of the estimate in which they stand. An *old-parent polynomial* is a bound $C_q\mu^{a_q}$; here $a_q$ denotes an exponent of this kind, which, like $C_q$, may change from one estimate to the next. Each statement is for $j$ large in terms of these, which raises only the starting index, since $K_j$ tends to infinity. We use the step of Subsection M.5.1 as it is applied in Section M.7: the parent $U$, with flow $X$ and $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$; the depth $P$ of (M.7.2); and the norms of Appendix M.D, at the label length $\ell_*$ and the phase length $h$. There $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $T_\infty(M.7.5) for $U$: $$\partial_t^qU =-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}\binom{q-1}i \partial_t^iU\otimes\partial_t^{q-1-i}U +\partial_t^{q-1}R_U .$$ The fields on the right are supported on frequencies at most $4\Lambda_U$ and involve time derivatives of order at most $q-1$. The periodic Leray projection is bounded on $C^{0,1/2}$, so (M.B.1) bounds $\|\partial_t^qU\|_\infty$ by an old-parent polynomial. By (M.B.1) again, for every $n\ge0$, $$\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{|\beta|=n}\|\partial^\beta\partial_t^iU\|_{L^\infty} &\le C_{n,q}\mu^{a_q}\Lambda_U^n\qquad(0\le i\le q),\\ \sum_{|\beta|=n}\|\partial^\beta\partial_t^iR_U\|_{L^\infty} &\le C_n\Lambda_U^n\lambda^{-5/2}\qquad(0\le i\le q-1). \end{aligned} \tag{2.1} \end{equation}$$ No time derivative of $R_U$ of order $q$ is used below. *Time derivatives of the coefficients.* With $D_t=\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla$, the $\ell$-fold material derivatives $D_t^\ell\nabla U$, $\ell\le q$, and $D_t^\ell R_U$, $\ell\le q-1$, are finite sums of products of at most $\ell+1$ of the fields in (2.1) and their spatial derivatives of order at most $\ell+1$, with exactly one factor from the second line in the case of $R_U$. They are supported on frequencies at most $4(q+1)\Lambda_U$. By (M.B.1), with $(q+1)\Lambda_U$ in place of $\Lambda$, their derivatives of order $m$ are at most $C_m(q+1)^m\Lambda_U^m$ times their suprema. Since $\Lambda_U=\mu^5\le\mathsf D$, this is the hypothesis of (M.5.7) with $C_m'=C_m(q+1)^m$. Since $\partial_t^\ell M=(D_t^\ell\nabla U)\circ X$, the composition estimates (M.5.7) and (M.5.8) of Proposition M.5.1 bound the norm $\|\partial_t^\ell M\|_{[n]}$, $\ell\le q$, at every order $n$ by an old-parent polynomial whose exponent depends on $q$, not on $n$. In the same way, since $\partial_t^\ell(R_U\circ X)=(D_t^\ell R_U)\circ X$, $$\begin{equation} \|\partial_t^\ell(R_U\circ X)\|_{[n]}\le C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/2} \qquad(0\le\ell\le q-1). \tag{2.2} \end{equation}$$ The remaining time jets follow from $\partial_t D_aX=MD_aX$, $((D_aX)^{-1})_t=-(D_aX)^{-1}M$, $(\kappa/\lambda)_t=-M^T\kappa/\lambda$ and the differentiated inverse identities of reciprocal coefficients, by a number of operations depending only on $q$, with Proposition M.5.1 and the product estimate of Lemma M.D.1. Thus $\|\partial_t^\ell\mathsf C\|_{[n]}\le C_q\mu^{a_q}$ for $0\le\ell\le q$ and for $\mathsf C$ among $(D_aX)^{\pm1}$, $M$, $\kappa/\lambda$, $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$, $K=(D_aX)^TD_aX$ and $\mathcal D=2(D_aX)^T\partial_t D_aX$. These bounds hold at every order $n$, so no label derivative is spent on a time derivative, and their exponents depend neither on the order, the level, the depth nor the new frequency parameter. They use the time derivatives of $U$ through order $q$ only. The construction is jointly smooth by Proposition M.5.4, so no time regularity of an unknown is assumed. *The two inverses with time derivatives.* At each order $n$, put $\mathcal J_l(f)=\sum_{i\le l}T^i\|\partial_t^if\|/i!$ with the norms $\|\cdot\|_{[n],\gamma}$ or $\|\cdot\|_{[n]}$. Time differentiation holds the label $a$ and the independent phase $s$ fixed; oscillations are divided by $\gamma$ afterwards, and means are unweighted. The time and phase suprema remain inside the sums over label multi-indices and phase orders. For $0\le\ell\le q$, extracting $\partial_t^\ell f$ from $\mathcal J_q(f)$ costs $\ell!T^{-\ell}$. By (M.3.1), $(\partial_t^\ell f)^\natural =(\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x)^\ell f^\natural$. The factors $1/i!$ turn the time Leibniz rule into a convolution, so Lemma M.D.1 holds for $\mathcal J_q$ with the same costs, and coefficient multipliers cost old-parent polynomials. A mean $B=D_aX v$ with source $f_{\rm m}$ satisfies, by (M.4.11) with $g=(D_aX)^Tf_{\rm m}$ and $\mathcal T=\mathbb PK$ on divergence-free label fields, $\mathcal Tv_t=\mathbb P(g-\mathcal Dv)$. Hence $$\mathcal T\partial_t^{l+1}v=\mathbb P\Big[\partial_t^l g -\sum_{i=0}^l\binom li(\partial_t^i\mathcal D)\partial_t^{l-i}v -\sum_{i=1}^l\binom li(\partial_t^iK)\partial_t^{l+1-i}v\Big],$$ whose right side contains $v$ and the source only to time order $l$. By the last assertion of Theorem M.4.2, the constant $A$ of (M.4.10) bounds the inverse of $\mathcal T$ on the divergence-free fields of $C^{0,1/2}$ at each time. Then (M.5.13) is condition (M.D.7) for the equation $\mathcal Tw=\mathbb PF$ with the coefficient $K$, and Lemma M.D.3 in its Hölder form inverts $\mathcal T$ in the norms $\|\cdot\|_{[n],1/2}$ at every order, with a constant that is an old-parent polynomial. Starting from the bound (M.5.14) for $v$, induction over $l\le q-1$ and (M.D.2) give, with the norms $\|\cdot\|_{[n]}$ on the left and $\|\cdot\|_{[n+1]}$ on the right, and independently of the depth, $$\begin{equation} \mathcal J_q(B)\le C_q\mu^{a_q}\mathcal J_{q-1}(f_{\rm m}). \tag{2.3} \end{equation}$$ Thus the mean velocity at time order $q$ uses its source only to time order $q-1$. No boundary condition is imposed on time derivatives; the undifferentiated solution keeps its actual initial trace. A transverse solution satisfies $V_t=-(\operatorname{Id}-2P_\kappa)MV+(\operatorname{Id}-P_\kappa)f$; the same induction from (M.5.21) bounds its time derivatives in $\mathcal J_q$ by an old-parent polynomial times $\mathcal J_q(f)$, and (M.5.16) bounds its pressure. On $[t_0,T]$ the leading oscillation $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$ solves this equation with $f=0$, and the cutoff of Subsection M.6.2 satisfies $|\widetilde\chi^{(l)}|\le C_lr^l$, with the rate $r$ of the comparison, and $r\le\mu$ by item 3 of the proof of Theorem M.7.1. With (M.5.20) and (M.5.22), the same induction bounds $A_1$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, their pressures and $R_{\widetilde\chi}=\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$ of (M.3.8) in the weighted $\mathcal J_q$ by an old-parent polynomial times $\lambda^{-5/4}$. *Sources and the expansion.* By (M.5.42), $\mathbf d\cdot B_i=\mathbf d\cdot C_i=0$ and the vanishing mixed phase means, the mean source is $$\bar f_p=-\operatorname{div}_{\mathbf d}\sum_{i+i'=p} (\langle Y_i\otimes Y_{i'}\rangle_s+B_i\otimes B_{i'})\qquad(p\ge3),$$ where $(\operatorname{div}_{\mathbf d}(\mathbf u\otimes \mathbf w))_\ell=\mathbf d_i(\mathbf u_i\mathbf w_\ell)$, and $\bar f_2$ is the same expression minus $R_U\circ X$, by (M.5.27). The time derivatives of the divergence term fall only on the fields and on the old coefficients in $\mathbf d$; no phase derivative or new wave vector appears. The mean sources are measured in $\mathcal J_{q-1}$, which (2.3) allows. The later sources contain the means $B_p$ themselves, and neither $\bar f_p$ nor a mean pressure. The oscillatory sources are differentiated in the expression for $(\partial_t+M)C[V]+\mathbf d\mathsf p$ in the proof of Lemma M.5.5, with (M.5.33), and in (M.5.28), which contain only coefficient multipliers, one label derivative, a normalized inverse wave vector, the existing factor $\kappa\partial_s$ and the fields; weights are carried as in Subsection M.5.5. By (2.2) and $T\le1$, the norm $\mathcal J_{q-1}(R_U\circ X)$ is at most an old-parent polynomial times $\lambda^{-5/2}$, which is (M.5.10) for these norms with that polynomial as a factor. The proof of Theorem M.5.6 uses the parent and the wave only through the bounds (M.5.8), (M.5.12), (M.5.21), (M.5.22), (M.5.10), (M.5.31) and (M.5.32), and through Lemma M.D.1. By the preceding paragraphs these hold in the norms $\mathcal J_q$, with the mean sources and the residual of the parent measured in $\mathcal J_{q-1}$, when each power of $\mathsf D$ on their right sides is replaced by an old-parent polynomial and the constants depend also on $q$. The residual of the parent enters that proof only through the mean source at level two, whose bound has a power of $\mathsf D$; the polynomial that replaces this power is taken at least as large as the one in the bound for the residual. The proof uses the hypothesis $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$ of the theorem only to absorb powers of $\mathsf D$. With an old-parent polynomial in their place the hypothesis reads $C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, which holds for $j$ large, since $\lambda=\mu^{K_j}$. Since time convolution does not change the factor $\lambda^{-2/3}$ per level, that proof therefore applies in $\mathcal J_q$, at every order, to the profiles $V_p$, $C_p$, $B_p$, the oscillatory pressures and the sources $f_p+f_p^S$, and gives (M.5.34)–(M.5.36) with each power $\mathsf D^C$ replaced by an old-parent polynomial $C_q\mu^{a_q}$. The mean pressures are not used. At the depth $P$, at each order $n$ and with constants $C_{n,P}$ that depend also on $q$, the same proof bounds $W_{\rm osc}$ by $C_{n,P}\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/4}$ in the weighted $\mathcal J_q$, the mean sum $\bar W$ by $C_{n,P}\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/2}$ in the unweighted one, and the remainder $R_P$ in the unweighted $\mathcal J_q$ by $C_{n,P}\lambda^{-5/4}\lambda^{-2P/3}$. The term $R_{\widetilde\chi}$ is at most an old-parent polynomial times $\lambda^{-5/4}$ in the weighted $\mathcal J_q$, and it vanishes, with its time derivatives, outside $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$. *Eulerian time derivatives.* By $\partial_t=(\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x)-U\cdot\nabla_x$, the Eulerian derivative $\partial_t^if^\natural$ of a profile $f$, for $i\le q$, is a finite sum of products of factors $\partial_t^l\partial^\beta U$, with $l\le q-1$ and $|\beta|\le q-1$, and one factor $\partial_x^{\beta'}(\partial_t^lf)^\natural$ with $l+|\beta'|\le q$. Lemma M.5.7 converts the bounds in $\mathcal J_q$ to Eulerian $C^{n,1/2}$ bounds of the last factor, spending $n+|\beta'|+1$ label and phase derivatives. Each of these derivatives costs $C\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2}\le\lambda^2$ for an oscillatory profile, and $C\mathsf D^C$, an old-parent polynomial, for a phase-independent one. The extraction costs $q!T^{-q}$, an old-parent polynomial, and the factors of $U$ cost $\Lambda_U=\mu^5$ for each derivative, by (2.1). For the phase-independent mean sum and fixed $(m,q)$ the whole cost is an old-parent polynomial. This preserves $\lambda^{-5/2}$: with a constant and an exponent that depend also on $m$, and for $j$ large, $$\begin{equation} \|\partial_t^q\bar W^\natural\|_{C([0,S_j];C^{m,1/2})} \le C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/2}\le\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}, \tag{2.4} \end{equation}$$ the last step because $\lambda=\mu^{K_j}$ and $K_j\to\infty$. For the approximate solution $V=U+W^\natural$ of step $j$ and its residual $R_V=(R_P+R_{\widetilde\chi})^\natural$, the same conversion gives, for $0\le i\le q$ and $0\le n\le P$, $$\begin{equation} \|\partial_t^iV\|_{C_tC^{n,1/2}}\le\lambda^{2(n+1)+\psi'_q},\qquad \|\partial_t^iR_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}} \le\lambda^{\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}, \tag{2.5} \end{equation}$$ with an exponent $\psi'_q\ge0$ independent of $j$ and $n$; the constants, which depend on $n$, $q$ and the depth, are bounded by $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})$. Indeed, the parent contributes at most $\lambda^{n+2}$ to the first bound, by (2.1) and $K_j\to\infty$. In the conversion, Leibniz’ rule distributes the $n$ derivatives over the factors of a product, and on a factor of $U$ each of them costs $\Lambda_U\le\lambda$. For the residual, the remainder $R_P$ carries $\lambda^{-2P/3}=\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, and on $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$ the conversion of Lemma M.5.7 carries the weight $\gamma\le Ce^{-L_j}=C\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, by (M.6.8) and (M.1.14). *The truncation difference.* Let $v_\Lambda=(S_{\Lambda_j}-\operatorname{Id})V$ be the truncation difference of Proposition M.5.11 at step $j$. We have $\partial_t^qv_\Lambda=(S_{\Lambda_j}-\operatorname{Id})\partial_t^qV$. By the tail bound (M.B.2) at the order $P$, whose constant is at most $\mu$, and by $\Lambda_j=\lambda^5$ and (2.5), for fixed $m$, $$\|\partial_t^qv_\Lambda\|_{C_tC^{m,1/2}} \le\mu\Lambda_j^{m-P}\lambda^{2(P+1)+\psi'_q} =\mu\lambda^{-3P+5m+2+\psi'_q}.$$ Since $\mu\le\lambda$ and $P\to\infty$, this is at most $\frac12\lambda^{-1}$ for $j$ large. Since $V=U_{j-1}+W^\natural$, $W=W_{\rm osc}+\bar W$ and $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, we have $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j=\bar W^\natural+v_\Lambda$, so this bound and (2.4) prove (1.2). *The residual and the new velocity.* It remains to prove Lemma 1.3 for $q$. Since $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, Lemma M.B.1 and (2.5) at $n=0$ give $\|\partial_t^iU_j\|_\infty\le\lambda^{\psi'_q+3}$ for $i\le q$, which is the first bound of (1.3) with $\psi_q=\psi'_q+3$. By (M.5.58), with $v=v_\Lambda$ and $S=S_{\Lambda_j}$, $$R_j=\mathbb P\bigl[SR_V +\operatorname{div}\bigl(v\otimes U_j+V\otimes v+(\operatorname{Id}-S)(V\otimes V)\bigr)\bigr].$$ Differentiate $i\le q$ times in time; the derivatives distribute over the products. The first term is bounded by (2.5). Every other term contains the operator $\operatorname{Id}-S$ applied to $\partial_t^lV$ or to $\partial_t^l(V\otimes V)$ with $l\le q$. By (2.5), the tail bound at the order $P$ and (M.5.59), these terms are at most $$C_{q,P}\Lambda_j^{2-P}\lambda^{4(P+1)+2\psi'_q} \le\lambda^{15-P+2\psi'_q} =\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-6}$$ in $C^{1,1/2}$, because $\Lambda_j=\lambda^5$, $C_{q,P}\le\lambda$ and $P=6K_{j+1}$. Altogether $\|\partial_t^iR_j\|_\infty \le\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ for $i\le q$, and $\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{3/2}$ for $j$ large, since $K_{j+1}\to\infty$. This proves the second bound of (1.3) at the time order $q$, and the induction is complete. $\square$ ### Note 3 Extension away from the origin *Proof of Theorem 1.1.* By Theorem M.7.1, on $[0,S_j]$ the oscillation $O_j$ is supported in the ball of radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ about the origin, and these radii tend to zero. Fix a compact set $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$. Only finitely many $O_j$ meet a neighborhood of $K$. For every fixed pair $(m,q)$, (1.2) and $\sum_j\lambda_j^{-1}<\infty$ give a summable bound for the remaining increments in $C^q([0,T_\infty];C^m(K))$. The finitely many earlier terms are smooth there because $S_j>T_\infty$. The sum therefore converges with every mixed derivative up to $T_\infty$ away from zero. Its limit equals $u$ before $T_\infty$ by Proposition M.8.1. Seeley’s extension theorem \[[1](#cite-Seeley), p. 625\], applied componentwise in boundary charts and patched with a locally finite spatial partition of unity, extends the field smoothly through $T_\infty$ away from zero. The main paper identifies $T_*=T_\infty$, which proves the theorem. $\square$ ### References of the note \[1\] R. T. Seeley, Extension of $C^\infty$ functions defined in a half space, *Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.* **15** (1964), 625–626. [doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0165392-8](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0165392-8).

rows.label: sec-finite-time-singularity-formation-for-the-three-dimensional-euler-equations
rows.text:
• Levent Alpöge
  • Tristan Buckmaster
  • Matei P. Coiculescu
We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time. The velocity remains bounded, while the vorticity magnitude at the origin tends to infinity. Away from the origin, the velocity and its time derivative have smooth spatial limits at the singular time. The construction uses localized Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks of a multi-scale construction.

# Reading the formal statements as mathematics

The paper is *Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations*, by Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster and Matei P. Coiculescu; the formal statements are theirs, at commit fd3a158. A definition specifies an object or a condition; an existence theorem supplies an object satisfying it. A step used inside a proof is not automatically a conclusion of the theorem it is linked to. Each card states its own hypotheses and conclusion.

rows.label: sec-norms-and-default-values
rows.text:
Vectors have the Euclidean norm and matrices its operator norm; $D_xu$ has entries $\partial_ju_i$. The $L^\infty$ quantities in Theorem 1.1 are essential suprema in $[0,\infty]$, and a nonnegative time integral may equal $\infty$. The endpoint $C^{0,1/2}$ norm is $\max(\|f\|_\infty,[f]_{1/2})$; the $C^{m,1/2}$ norm used for convergence sums the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of the derivatives through order $m$; Appendix D sums weighted coordinate derivatives. These conventions are not interchangeable inside an estimate, and a supremum in time of a spatial norm is not a space-time norm.

Some operations have default values. Division by zero gives zero, so $v/|v|$ is a unit vector only when $v\ne0$. The square root of a negative number is zero; $\log0=0$ and $\log(-x)=\log x$. A real supremum of an unbounded set is zero; an integral of a nonintegrable function is zero. Derivative orders and schedule exponents are nonnegative integers, and subtraction of such indices stops at zero. None of these defaults supplies a missing hypothesis: each card says where positivity, regularity and integrability enter.

rows.label: sec-the-endpoint-problem
rows.text: Put $F=D_aX$, $M=(D_xU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. The hypothesis $H^\#\le I$ bounds a quadratic form from above and allows large negative eigenvalues. The unknowns satisfy $Kv-\int_0^t\Omega v+L=c+\nabla_a\phi$, $v=z_t$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_az=0$, with $c$ independent of time and divergence free. Uniqueness concerns $z$, $v$, $c$ and the pressure gradient; the potential is fixed only by its zero mean. The velocity bound keeps the source norm, $\|v\|\le A\|L\|$. The formal theorem allows weaker coefficient regularity than the paper but keeps ellipticity and displacement coercivity.

rows.label: sec-the-sequence-and-the-terminal-time
rows.text: The indices follow the paper: $\lambda_0=N$, $q_1=1$, $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$, $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$; the maximum rule picks the greatest admissible order. Constants chosen before the data are uniform in those data. The real cutoff uses the real part of a spectral kernel, and its identification with the multiplier uses an even symbol, as the paper's radial symbol is. Appendix D's weighted estimates need bounds for $f/\gamma$; positivity of $\gamma$ alone does not give them. Local limits of $u$ and $\partial_tu$ are distinct from a smooth extension through the terminal time; the auxiliary theorem supplies such an extension away from the origin and imposes no Euler equation after the terminal time.

rows.label: sec-the-torus-and-the-time-interval
rows.text:
The torus is $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. Fields are integer-periodic functions on $\mathbb R^3$ or, in the endpoint spaces, functions on the quotient. Integrals and essential suprema use the unit cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3$, of volume one. Avoiding the torus origin means avoiding every point of $\mathbb Z^3$ on the covering space. The lift uses the Euclidean distance and the endpoint quotient the maximum of the three circle distances; their Hölder seminorms are equivalent, not equal.

Functions have values at every real time, but Euler, smoothness and uniqueness are asserted only on the stated interval. A classical solution is jointly smooth on $[0,T_*)\times\mathbb R^3$ with $0<T_*<\infty$; maximality excludes a smooth Euler extension agreeing in velocity on a longer interval. The approximate stages live on closed intervals $[0,S_j]$, and their activation times tend to $T_\infty<S_j$. Derivatives at an included endpoint are one-sided.

rows.label: sec-the-wave-and-its-frame
rows.text:
For nonzero perpendicular $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ the frame is $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$. At $t_0$ freeze $\sigma=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$, $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2>0$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$, with $B$ the older gradient; put $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$, $S=\sigma/r$ and $\tau=r(t-t_0)$. The reference angle $\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ is not the actual wave direction, and the reference zero need not locate the actual amplitude maximum. Amplitude normalization specifies an attained maximum, not only an upper bound.

A profile $f(t,a,s)$ has independent label and phase variables; physical evaluation substitutes $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$ and $s=k_*\cdot a$, and a physical force becomes $f(t,X(t,a))$ in labels. The hierarchy separates exact algebraic cancellation, solvability of the mean and transverse equations, and quantitative bounds; its stability assumption controls every transverse homogeneous solution, not only the selected wave.

rows.label: sec-what-a-comparison-means
rows.text: **Same**: the quoted assertion agrees after the stated translation. **Stronger**: the formal statement has fewer hypotheses, more conclusions or a sharper bound, and the card names the difference. **Weaker**: the converse. **Different**: neither direction fits, for example when a definition or a final estimate is linked to a sentence about a construction or an intermediate identity. A judgment concerns the quoted assertion only; a shared name or number is not evidence of equivalence.
